utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the staff members present here in the courtroom. The Trial Chamber will read out two oral decisions. From what I understood, Mr. Karnavas needs an extra few minutes to talk about a particular subject, and then we shall address the question of witness protection. Mr. Scott will then have the floor, and I hope he will not exceed 15 minutes. Defence counsel will also have 15 minutes, and after that, we shall bring the witness into the courtroom for this afternoon. The first oral decision that has been rendered is as follows and relates to those exhibits which were presented through the Witness BY. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit these exhibits on the grounds that they have a certain probative value and a certain relevance. I shall read them slowly P 08543, P 09147, P 09149, P 09155. The Trial Chamber would like to remind you that documents IC 066, IC 067, IC 068 and IC 069 tendered by the Prosecution have been admitted under seal on the 27th of October. Of course the IC numbers usually have three zeros, so it should read IC 00066. In addition, P 09151, P 09152. There's a mistake on line 3. P 09151, P 09152, P 09153, P 09154 and P 09163 have been admitted pursuant to an oral decision on the 30th of September 2006. The Trial Chamber reminds you that documents IC 00070, IC 00071 and IC 00072 tendered by the Defence have been admitted under seal on the 27th of October, 2006. The document 3D 00475 also tendered by the Defence has -- was admitted following an oral decision on the 2nd of November 2006. Second oral decision, which is a longer decision: Oral decision relating to the joint motion filed by the Defence and relating to list of exhibits filed by the Prosecution before the witnesses's testimonies. On the 16th October, 2006, the Defence has filed a written motion relating to the exhibits which the Prosecution files before each witness testimony. As a rule, the Defence counsel asks the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to make sure that this exhibit list matches the 4th of September, 2006, charts. Subsidiarily, it asks the Prosecution to file its exhibit list which it intends to present through witness, 30 days before the witness appears in court. On the 19th of October, 2006, the Prosecution objected to this request. After having reviewed the submissions by both parties, the Trial Chamber renders the following decision: The Trial Chamber would like to remind you, first of all, that the charts filed on the 4th of September, 2006 by the Prosecution were provided in order to assist the Chamber as well as Defence counsel to establish a connection between the witnesses and the exhibits, on the one hand, and the allegations set forth in the indictment on the other hand. The Trial Chamber would like to remind you, that according to the decisions rendered on the 3rd and 13th of July, 2006, it has charged the Prosecution to disclose to the Defence counsel all the exhibits it intends to present through a witness two weeks before the witness appears in court. Moreover, according to the decision rendered -- oral decision on the 21st of August, 2006, the Trial Chamber has stated that the Prosecution should, as a rule, submit to Defence counsel only those documents which are mentioned in the 65 ter list. However, it has given the Prosecution the possibility to submit the documents which are not mentioned in the 65 ter list. If the Prosecution is able to justify the latter, i.e., that they are essential to determining the case, the Prosecution must also justify the reasons why these documents are filed at such a late stage and must also tell the Defence counsel why the latter were not mentioned in the 65 ter list. Lastly, the Trial Chamber would like to remind you, that according to the oral decision rendered on the 24th of August, 2006, it has -- it realised that the proofing of a witness could produce new evidence and allow the Prosecution to extend its examination-in-chief, thus enabling the Defence to better prepare its cross-examination. The Trial Chamber has then decided that the Prosecution should instantly disclose to Defence counsel, but as well as all the legal officers of the Chamber, any new piece of information that would have resulted or occurred after the proofing of a witness. This measure should enable the Trial Chamber to rule on any objections which are likely to be made by the Defence counsel. This oral decision on the 24th of August, 2006, did not, however, settle the question of the communication or disclosure of new exhibits that could stem from a witness -- from the proofing of the witness. However, the Trial Chamber has usually applied those principles laid out in the decision when it comes to taking a decision on the exhibits. Therefore, the Prosecution has told the Defence counsel and the Chamber that every time a witness proofing led to a an amendment of exhibits list, it would inform the latter. The Trial Chamber is therefore able to take an instant decision on such an amendment of the rights of the accused. The Trial Chamber feels that there is no particular reason for wanting to change what has already been established in practice. It feels that various work tools that have been provided to Defence counsel are there to assist it in an efficient and fair manner and so as to properly prepare for its cross-examination. Therefore, the Prosecution is responsible for disclosing the list of exhibits relating to a particular witness two weeks before this witness comes to court. The proofing of a witness may call for an amendment of the list on the part of the Prosecution, and this is exceptional. The implications of such an amendment shall be reviewed by the Chamber on a case-by-case basis. Upon reviewing the matter, the Trial Chamber will look into these last-minute changes and check that the latter do not interfere with the good preparation of the cross-examination by the Defence counsel, thus making sure that fairness and efficiency are being abided by. Consequently, the Trial Chamber rejects the application made by the Defence counsel. I should like to add the following comment: The question raised by the Defence counsel is due to the fact that, on several occasions, the Defence counsel discover documents, particularly when documents stem from the proofing of the witness. I have had occasion to mention this on several occasions. As a rule, the Trial Chamber, and more so the Defence counsel, should be able to react instantly when such documents are being presented. As the Defence counsel should be familiar with all the documents presented through a witness, this should be no cause for surprise. I would also like to specify that the Bench sometimes discover these documents when we walk into the courtroom. Sometimes these are documents which are a hundred pages long, which, however, does not prevent us from putting questions to the witness. So when a document comes in at the last moment, any professional lawyer should be able to put questions to the witness. And when the Defence counsels need to cross-examine the witness, they should be able to do the same. As a rule, the following procedure should be adopted: The Prosecution should disclose all the exhibits before the witness enters the courtroom, and we should only find ourselves in such a situation in exceptional circumstances, in which case the Trial Chamber will rule on it on a case-by-case basis. Mr. Karnavas, I think you wanted to say a few words. But before you take the floor, in order to organise the hearing for this afternoon and tomorrow afternoon as far as the witness from the French -- from the Spanish Battalion is concerned, I don't wish to quote any names, I think initially you had -- the Prosecution had planned to hear the witness for four hours. We feel that three hours is ample time. The Defence counsel will also have three hours. So it's three hours for each. Three hours for the Prosecution, three hours for Defence counsel. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Just very briefly. As you well know, on November 10th the Prosecution filed a motion regarding 92 bis (A) and (B) material. Several statements, I believe there are 15 of them -- the Prosecution wishes to introduce on the basis that these are cumulative and/or corroborative of other evidence. Now, if you look at the motion, the Prosecution does lay out as to why it may be cumulative or corroborative vis-a-vis the particular witness that has already appeared before us in viva voce testimony. However, a close reading of the motion shows that there's insufficient information to show as to why a particular witness has cumulative or -- or corroborative testimony. In other words, there's no details other than just saying it refers to this witness and just the buzzwords cumulative and corroborative. We feel that's insufficient information in order for us to respond, particularly in light of the Prosecution's motion with respect to paragraph 9, wherein the Prosecution says that the Defence, if it does wish to cross-examine any particular witness, should specify the reasons as to why they need to question a particular witness. So in order for us to respond in that fashion, we need more information from the Prosecution, and so we would like some sort of a oral decision today whether you just wish us to respond or whether you will be requiring the Prosecutor to provide more information. And I don't want to get ahead of the motion itself and put our response orally, but frankly, if the information is cumulative and if the information is already corroborative, there's no need for it. If it's -- why do you need to hear cumulative information? So in any event, if we could have some sort of a ruling, because we do need to response, I believe, by -- by the end of this week to this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Prosecution has filed a motion which I read this morning. These are not 15 92 bis witnesses but 11 all in all. Whether it's 11 or 15, it all amounts to the same. But if I remember correctly, those submissions filed by the Prosecution, mention is made of all the viva voce witnesses. If Defence counsel wish to respond in writing, you have eight days. Of course, we will look at the written statements of these witnesses and compare them with the witness -- with the viva voce witness testimonies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. And I understand that, Mr. President, but it would appear that the Prosecution is shifting the work onto the Defence and the burden onto the Defence to show why we need to cross-examine. It's not sufficient, as far as we're concerned, for them to simply say it's cumulative it or corroborative because it refers to a particular witness. They should demonstrate exactly what is cumulative or corroborative from their standpoint. And also, as I indicated earlier, if indeed it is cumulative, why on earth do we need it? Normally, that's the whole purpose of excluding evidence, because it's cumulative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not going to be spending too much time on this issue. As I have mentioned to you, you have 10 days and even an additional 4 days, which is two weeks, to respond in writing to the 11 statements for which the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the deadlines you mentioned for response, it was eight and now it seems to be 14. As far as I can remember, on the basis of the Rules of Evidence, I think that we have 14 days for a response, and you have just said 14 days, so that's fine. We have an fortnight to respond. Your Honour, could we, in the course of the day today and you will tell us when, put forward some of the exhibits that go with Witness Agic and also for Idrizovic and a piece of information that there was an MFI document as well. So when the chance arises, I'd like to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will look into the matter at a later stage. Now we have to address the question of protective measures. Let me remind you that the last time Defence counsel Mr. Ciocha [as interpreted] and the Prosecution wanted to address the issue, as you know, protective measures are governed by Rule 75 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence and that leeway is not very great. The Trial Chamber does not have much room to manoeuvre. And when we are talking about representatives from various governments, an example which is a well-known example, General Clark had testified under protective measures. After that, the -- the United States government lifted the protective measures and the hearing was therefore rendered public. It is important to protect the identity of some of the witnesses, particularly when some women have been sexually abused. Also when some witnesses are exposed to a potential danger. I have asked the Witness and Victims Unit how many witnesses have actually been granted protective measures. I believe that in all the witnesses that have testified here, 40 per cent have been granted protective measures. I know that in addition to this, in some cases, fewer protective measures have been granted. I looked up -- looked into the matter in the Krajisnik case. I know that out of 25 witnesses that had been requested by Defence counsel, only three have been granted protective measures. These are measures which are take own a case-by-case basis and which are decided upon by the Trial Chamber with the discretionary powers they have. Mr. Scott, before I give you the floor, just for a split second, I would like to move into private session, please, and then I will give the floor back to you. This will not take very long.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are currently in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Scott, you have the floor for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm having trouble with my microphone today. May it please the Court, I just want to respond ever so briefly to the issues raised by Mr. Karnavas because -- with the greatest of respect, I don't think it's fair, appropriate for one party to get up and address an issue and for the other party not to be heard at least briefly. On the 92 bis submission, Your Honour, as the -- as the Chamber well knows, the Prosecution has stated, since the beginning of this trial and since before the beginning of the trial, that a major part of its trial strategy and indeed in order -- excuse me, Judge Prandler. Indeed in order to have any chance, and I emphasise the word "any chance," to present our evidence in the time allowed by the Chamber will require, and I say in my estimate will require, not might, not may, will require an extensive use of Rule 92 bis evidence as we believe the Rules provide for, that there has been a bit of a sea change in the practice of the Tribunal in the last few years and the efficiencies and facilities that provided by that rule should be used to the maximum extend of course consistent with due process. Now, we believe our submission meets all the requirements. I would invite and implore the Chamber not to impose more technical requirements on the Prosecution as to the types of showings and filings that will be required. The situation is simply this: The Prosecution has called fairly extensive viva voce and Rule 92 ter evidence with all that evidence being subject to full courtroom cross-examination by both the Judges and by the Defence. There is then a remaining body of evidentiary witness evidence material which, because of the time limitations, et cetera, cannot possibly be put before the Chamber in a viva voce or other way. Therefore, we are putting it forward. All of it relates to the crime base area that has preceded it. In this case, Prozor. We believe our submissions make all the required showings. There is a detailed chart and summary and a detailed chart showing the -- once again, the paragraphs and counts of the indictment to which it relates. Secondly, and again, Your Honour, very quickly. The Defence has said they need more information in order to be able to respond and they specifically raise that in connection with the acts and conduct of the accused. Your Honour, we respectfully disagree. The witness statements themselves are very clear as to what the evidence of that witness is or would be. If, in the view of counsel, if in the view of counsel, they implicate the acts and conduct of the accused within the meaning of the Rule, within the meaning of the Rule, and the Tribunal has taken a fairly narrow view of acts and conduct of the accused, then the Defence should state that clearly and say, "We object to this particular evidence of this particular witness coming in because we think that it unfairly implicates acts and conduct of the accused." And we've set that out in our submissions, our position, and we do not believe, respectfully, that the Defence needs any more information in order to be able to identify those parts of it which they contend go to acts and conduct of the accused. Thirdly, Your Honour, Mr. Karnavas, and it doesn't entirely surprise me, because we come from the same system, and in our system, cumulative is generally considered a bad word and not a good word in terms of what is cumulative. A better word, I submit in my humble personal opinion, would be corroboration. I guess one man's accumulativeness is another man's corroboration. The Rule is quite clear, in the sense in which it is used, and that is in Rule 92 bis (A) (B), it says this, "Factors in favour of admitting evidence" and then sub (A), "is of a cumulative nature." So the Rules clearly say that a positive factor that favours -- in fact favours admission is that it is cumulative in this sense. And cumulative in the sense that viva voce and other evidence has already been led, and that which then provides the basis for the application of the Rule. I apologise for taking the Chamber's time to address those points but I thought that some abbreviated response was appropriate and I appreciate the Court for hearing me. Thank you. As to the issue of witness protection, and I will be brief on this, I think the points are really rather straightforward frankly. There are three interests, I suggest, that are implicated by these matters in the courtroom: One is the interest of the accused; one is the interest of the victim and witness -- or witness; and three, the third interest is the interest of the public in seeing and hearing the evidence in these proceedings. As to the first, Your Honour, I submit -- we respectfully submit that as to the interest of the accused, these are fully addressed and virtually not implicated at all by protective measures, that is, the Defence themselves -- the Defence lawyers, the accused sitting in court, get full disclosure. The protective measures in fact have absolutely nothing to do with the accused. They have the witness name. They have the full statements. They have everything. In the courtroom, they have the full opportunity to confront the witness. They have the full opportunity to cross-examine the witness. And it's the Prosecution position, Your Honour, that at least in the vast majority of instances, of course, there can always be some exception, but in the vast majority of instances, frankly, the rights and the interest of the accused are not implicated at all by protective measures. They have the full right to cross-examine. All these men are here. They can all see the witness in the courtroom. They know exactly who the witness -- we're not talking about secret witnesses in some remote courtroom. They can all see the witness sitting right here. They have the real name. They have it way in advance. Their interests are not implicated at all. The public, of course, would like to hear as much of the evidence as possible, and we understand that, but in the most -- again, in most instances, the protective measures that are usually most -- most usually requested, based on long years of experience and also borne out by this particular trial, is for the witness to be given a pseudonym and facial image distortion. Now, what are the implications of that for public testimony? And again virtually none. The public gets to hear virtually the entire evidence of the witness. It goes out of the courtroom virtually a hundred per cent of its content unless it is something very specific that would specifically identify the witness. So what are the interests of the public hearing the evidence? And do they hear the evidence when a witness testifies with a pseudonym and with facial image distortion? Yes, they hear -- the public hears virtually every word. The third interest that has to be dealt with is the -- it the protection, of course, of the victim witness itself -- him or herself. Now, let me start by saying one thing, which I don't think we can fully address today. If the Chamber wants to get into it in a more substantial way, then I submit respectfully that some additional time and resources would have to be devoted to the question. Various statements have been made to suggest that these concerns can't be genuine. They can't be real, these concerns expressed by the witness. Your Honours, these are the concerns, these are the heartfelt concerns of the witnesses who bring them before the Chamber. These are not the Prosecution's positions. These are not the Prosecution's statements. These are what the witness themselves come for. And a witness, for example, comes into court and says I haven't even told anyone I'm here. My employer doesn't know, most of my family doesn't know. To me, Your Honour, when a witness -- someone takes that many significant steps, that's one example. That shows to me the witness takes it seriously. It isn't just some afterthought. It's because the witness is concerned about the situation. And with the greatest of respect to the efforts of this Tribunal and the efforts of the international community in Bosnia-Herzegovina over the past 13 or 14 years, it remains far from an ideal situation, far from an ideal situation. You can look at any international report -- after any international report, whether it's the European Community, whether it's the OSCE, whatever, significant concerns continue. So simply -- well, with respect, Your Honour, I don't think we can simply be dismissive when the witnesses come in and express these concerns. Finally, Your Honour, then it leads us to how do we balance out the rights of the victim and witness to reasonable protective measures and the interest of the public in hearing the evidence. And I submit, Your Honours, that in 99 per cent of the cases, a pseudonym and facial image distortion is a completely, a completely fair balance of those interests. The public gets virtually a hundred per cent of the evidence and the witness gets some protection. And we submit that that should be when those types of measures are requested, they should be given with reasonable flexibility. I would invite the Chamber, if the Chamber has continuing concerns about this and if the Chamber has any concerns that our position might be tainted by the adversary nature or our advocacy, I invite the Chamber to consult directly with the Victims and Witness Section, hear what they have to say. They're not a part of the Prosecution. They're not part of the Defence. And they can give the Chamber their position and their concerns over witness protection. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott, for what you've said. Mr. Stewart, you asked for the floor and I'm giving it to you. You have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The -- the first point is to say that the -- it's not the Defence's position, I don't believe it has been and I don't believe it will be the position that we say that the concerns expressed by witnesses when they come to court are not genuine. That misrepresents the Defence's submission and their position. We recognise that witnesses's concerns are honest and genuine. What we question is whether there is a sufficient objective basis for those concerns to justify interference with the basic right to a public and fair trial, and that will, I'm confident, remain the Defence position throughout in relation to such matters. Second, and this is a point of real importance, it is absolutely false to say that the accuseds' interests are not implicated at all provided that he is able to -- we're talking about he's in this case, the defendants -- he is able to know the identity of the witness himself and have his counsel know the identity of the witness and know the facts on which to cross-examine. That fundamentally undermines and contradicts the basic notion of a public trial. And Your Honours are extremely familiar with the Statute, but Article 22 expressly gives the accused the entitlement to a fair and public hearing. So right at the highest level in the Statute that right is recognised. And the reasons without elaborating, the well-known reasons why all the developed open systems of justice have public trials with very limited exceptions, is that it is regarded as fundamentally important that when witnesses come along and say what they've got to say, whether it's an accusation or implicitly an accusation against the defendant or whether it's in favour of the defendant or whether it's neither, that what they say is subject to scrutiny and scrutiny outside the courtroom. And unless there are exceptional circumstances, they should know that their neighbours, they should know that their colleagues may find out and can easily find out what they say, because that public scrutiny is absolutely fundamental. It's a critical check on the truthfulness and veracity of evidence. So the very starting point that Mr. Scott puts forward there is fundamentally incorrect. It is not, and it can be very misleading, to take those three elements, the accused, the victims and witness, the public interest and suggest that there's some sort of balancing exercise among those three especially when he almost discards the first of those interests anyway. The position is on analysis that you start with a strong presumption that there should be a public trial. I've said that in all developed systems, you start with a public trial and all developed open-justice systems do allow in camera or similar restrictions in the interests of justice, but we all know that a very high test is set. The reason why we have frequent protective measures before this Tribunal is not that the test is lower, it's that the very circumstances in which cases come to trial here and the difficulties and dangers and instability in the region mean that those circumstances are going to arise more often and that high test will be met more often than is familiar in domestic tribunals but is not a lower test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I think the Prosecution is absolutely right and what it says is completely in accordance with case law if it speaks of a balancing of interests. Second, the fact that the identity of witnesses is not revealed to the public does not diminish the granting of the right to a fair trial because -- to a public trial. It is a right of the accused. It is not a right of the public, unless you can show me other case law of an international body. It is not, and it is not either the purpose that the public can control whether the witness says the truth or not. This is for the Defence, and the Defence knows the identity. The Defence can watch the witness as the witness gives his or her statement, and I think this is -- this is absolutely sufficient if there are reasons for fear of the witnesses, and we have concluded in several cases that it is indeed the case. So I'm not convinced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, I can try to convince you by clarifying what I'm saying, because I can see there may be a gap between what I'm trying to say and what Your Honour understands I'm saying. I was submitting that to talk about a balancing exercise on those three elements can be misleading. I'm not saying -- I'm not saying, Your Honour, that in the end, starting with a public trial, as the basic principle and then looking to see whether there are sufficient circumstances to justify that encroachment. I'm not saying that there is no sort of balancing exercise there because, of course, there is. I accept that. You balance the need for the protection of that particular witness against that fundamental starting point principle of a fair trial. So of course there is a weighing and a balancing and I hope that clarifies what I am saying there. So far as the accused concerned, it is under the Statute it is -- it's the accused's right to a public hearing. Inherent in the whole system of justice is a strong public interest in having public hearings, but the strong public interest is in having a fair trial in this context. And again, Your Honour, with respect, I don't believe we're -- we differ really on this. In this context, the question is whether there are sufficiently strong circumstances established to encroach upon the openness of the evidence being given. If there are, then that's fair. That's a fair result and it doesn't impinge on the fair trial. But what -- I also wish to make it clear, the Defence will not oppose applications for protective measures in this case where there is credible material showing substantial objective risks. None of us has any interest in exposing witnesses to undue objective risks, but it is important that sensibilities, and this is again a difficult submission which I try to make as clear as I can in case it's misunderstood. When witnesses have extreme and understandable sensibilities about appearing, when victims have those sensibilities and they have suffered terrible things, all human sympathy goes towards that victim and giving evidence is unlikely to be anything other than a very hard experience. But where there is no risk to the witness outside the courtroom, it can only be in the most extreme circumstances seriously impinging upon the health or stability of the witness that one is justified in saying that because of those sensibilities the witness must be allowed to have protective measures to give evidence anonymously. Many witnesses entirely understandably would prefer that and those true in many domestic trials as well, but that is not the test. What -- what we do say is that responsible consideration of whether protective measures are justified, case by case, requires, first of all, conscientious inquiry as to the potential risks, and the objective justification. And the Victims and Witnesses Unit are a -- of course, a valuable source and they are enshrined in the Rules as a source, but with the greatest respect to Victims and Witnesses, it's important that their information is carefully examined because of course they are quite naturally close to witnesses and there to protect the witnesses. So they are bound to have a sympathetic view towards the witnesses and that's not in any way -- that's not impugning anybody's good faith. It's just a perfectly natural aspect of their work. Secondly, there should be clear presentation of that material - and this next point is crucially important - in time for all parties and the Trial Chamber to give it proper consideration. What has happened in this case is that an unsatisfactory practice has developed of the reasons and the material being given at the last minute. The Defence, we are after all six defendants, Your Honours quite rightly prefer us to get together and try to discuss and agree our position. We can't do that when the material is given to us at the very last minute. We're asked to react hurriedly. The Trial Chamber doesn't have the benefit of proper consideration of proper submissions in relation to the matter. So what we are suggesting, as a practical course, having set out those principles, is that the -- that the Trial Chamber might consider guidelines to require, save in circumstances where for good reason it simply can't be done, require advance notice of an application and supporting facts before a witness comes to The Hague. It may be that the reaction on the Defence side will then be to say, yes, we agree, we support. It may be that we would say, no, the material you have produced we say is inadequate. Then the Prosecution -- let's assume it's that way round. It will be the same the other way round when it comes to the Defence case, if we get that far. They would have the opportunity to supplement that information. We will waste less time in court because it -- there will be less and less need, in fact, there should be only a relatively rare need then to have to explore the matter with the witness when the witness comes into court. Your Honour, interestingly enough, Your Honour did mention the Krajisnik case and perhaps since Your Honour mentioned, I might be permitted to mention it, because, after all, I was in it throughout the trial. Of course, a higher proportion of Prosecution witnesses who came from the localities received protective measures because naturally Prosecution witnesses tended to include more victims. But that practice of advance application and that practice of the Defence being given ample time by the Prosecution to consider the material was adopted very early in the trial, and so one doesn't need to look at the individual decisions. Some -- some were successful. Most of the Prosecution applications were successful as it happens. But, Your Honours, in our submission, they were responsibly made generally and they were genuine victims. We didn't always agree but that's by the way. But, Your Honour, that practice does help the Trial Chamber enormously, we suggest. We do as part of that, and this is really my last point, Your Honour, we do then have some slight concerns about the way in which this matter is raised with witnesses, because we're not there and Your Honours can't control and give detailed guidelines to counsel and it wouldn't be proper. You trust us to do our jobs. But if a witness is asked, "Do you want to give your evidence in public? Would you rather give your evidence in private?" We do have a slight feeling that the question might be asked in that way. You're only going to get one answer in many cases. The right way, we suggest, for anybody asking a witness is to ask whether there is a risk, a starting point. If you do give evidence -- explains the witness, that normally speaking, they give evidence in public and ask if you do give evidence in public, is that going to cause a serious risk to you or your family or anybody else and then one would get much quicker to the heart of the matter. Everybody would be helped, and in the cases where protective measures are justified, they get given. But it stands a much better chance then of having the right decision and achieving. And with great respect to His Honour Judge Trechsel, I used this phrase, achieving the right balance between the starting point of a public trial and those cases where protective measures are genuinely justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Stewart, I'd like to say something at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because your intervention was highly interesting and we're all interested in theory here, of course, but it made me a little sad because, in a way, it would seem that you have not understood yet the efforts made by the Trial Chamber to establish this right balance, to strike the proper balance between the interests of the accused and the interests of the victims and, of course, the witnesses that come here to contribute to the furtherance of justice. You referred to the Statutes and to the Rules of Procedure which advocate a public hearing, and we are, of course, aware of all that. But at the same time, you also raise the necessity to ensure the protection of witnesses pursuant to Rule 69 of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and that is precisely what the Trial Chamber is trying to do. The Trial Chamber has close contacts with the witness and victims unit in order to be apprised of the situation on the ground. And also, you were able to following the efforts made by the Trial Chamber to ensure with the OTP that if there is -- the witnesses run any risk, that protective measures be taken and that the Trial Chamber rules in their favour. And that is why I'm saying that your expose has made me a little sad because it doesn't seem to me that you understand the efforts made by the Trial Chamber to strike this balance. And I also wanted to say a moment ago to the Prosecutor that they should provide the Trial Chamber with all the relevant information about a witness seeking protective measures and otherwise, because we have had cases here where -- when the proceedings were under way, we learnt of things we hadn't been told of in advance. And having said that, what you said was very interesting, but I should like to say that the Trial Chamber is fully aware of that, and we -- rest assured that we are fully aware of the situation and that we shall, of course, be asking the OTP to follow along those lines, to follow suit. So I don't want -- I don't think we should take up more time on that issue, or at least not more than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. President, I apologise the fact that your -- like restrictive viewing at a football match, I'm behind the pillar here, but I would if I may like to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Stewart please speak into the microphone as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to change microphones, Your Honour. I hope that works. Your Honour, I'm addressing His Honour Judge Mindua directly. Your Honour, I'm sad to be misunderstood. Your Honour has heard a criticism of the Trial Chamber which was not there in my submissions. When we look at what has happened recently and the particular points mentioned by the president earlier today, that in fact illustrates that occasionally the Trial Chamber is faced with a difficulty and is put at a disadvantage in having to make these decisions. So, Your Honour, my submissions did not involve any suggestion that in some wholesale way the Trial Chamber is failing in its duty. The suggestion is that a different approach and a more helpful approach and a more timely approach in producing the information and following the President's injunction that all the information should be put -- should be put before the Court will indeed help you even better to reach the right decision. And so far as the Victims and Witness Unit is concerned, of course they are there to be consulted. We do suggest that it is of the utmost importance that information coming to the Trial Chamber, to the Prosecution, should also come to the Defence so that we all have the same information at our disposal on which submissions can be made if decisions can be made. But I hope Your Honour will, with those few comments, I hope Your Honour will see my assurance that that criticism I hope to alleviate the sadness of that criticism which Your Honour heard is not in fact there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. We have heard the observations made by both sides, by the Prosecution and what Mr. Stewart had to say, and the others, and the Judges will deliberate. For the moment, we'll go on with our regular proceedings and bear in mind all the ideas put forward by you on the possibility of asking the witness, before the start, to tell the witness that the proceedings are public, and if they do not wish their testimony to go public that they should state the reasons for that. So we shall be examining all the proposals put forward, and we'll give you a ruling and tell you what we think. Now, as far as the next witness is concerned, there's no problem with that because she has already been granted measures of that type, and since she was granted protective measures, she's going to continue under the same regime. We're going to have the witness brought into the courtroom in a few moments, but before we do that, we're going to have the blinds lowered. And once the blinds have been lowered, we shall go ahead with all the formalities and go back into open session with the protective measures in place. So we're now going to lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just be heard for a second while the witness is coming in. I just wanted to supplement what was said which Mr. Stewart and by -- by the Prosecution. I think by and large, we're not far apart, and we always rely on the Trial Chamber to use its discretion, its wise discretion. And it has been wise in the past, so I don't want there to be any misunderstanding that there had been any complaints and we do take on board. I just want to make sure that no one on the trial Bench or the Prosecution thinks that the Defence does not recognise the particular needs of witnesses. We're not heartless, and I think that's sometimes, because of the adversarial nature, Defence lawyers are portrayed as being overly aggressive, mean, uncaring, and what have you. I don't want that impression to be left with the Trial Chamber. We're very mindful of that. My main concern is when there are closed sessions. And the only thing I ask is that we use the least restrictive measure, that's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. For a minute, we are going into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with this background in mind, Witness CA, and again we are now in public session, so whatever you say will be going outside the courtroom. Apart from that, can you tell the Chamber, several days prior to the 17th of April, 1993, had check-points been set up around the entrances and exits of the village of Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who set those check-points up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats set them up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say that Doljani is essentially divided between an upper part of the village and a lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to the people in the lower part of the village, were they still able to leave the village notwithstanding the existence of these check-points and, if so, tell the Judges why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were able to but not by road. They had to go through the woods. They couldn't get out by road, and they had to do it by night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the people in the upper part of Doljani? Were they able to leave the area under -- once the check-points were set up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't pass through. They wouldn't be allowed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did any members of the community of Doljani try to pass through and leave Doljani during this time through any of the check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and they were turned back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Chamber that, notwithstanding that, did there come a time around the 16th of April that a number of Muslims from the lower part of the village were in fact able to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what happened in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But they were turned back. They were turned back, too, from the check-point. They had set out and then they returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Notwithstanding that, did there come a time that some of the Muslims were successful in leaving Doljani at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th, by night, they left across the hills. But those who tried the real road couldn't get out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the ones that -- the Muslims who were able to get out on the night of the 16th of April, approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know the number. Several. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I realise this is some time ago, but assist us as much as you can, please. Are we talking about five or six, or are we talking about a hundred, or give us -- can you give us an estimate of the number of the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about a hundred of them. Certainly not less. Maybe more. Civilians, women, children, men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now -- if we can go into private session for one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For a few moments we are going to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, without saying anything more about your particular location in the village, can you tell the Judges, were you and your family able to get out of the Doljani area prior to the time that the conflict broke out on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, once these approximately 100 Muslims had left Doljani on the night of the 16th, approximately how many Muslims remained in Doljani after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the same number that left. Around a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to direct your attention specifically to the morning of the 17th of April, 1993. Can you please tell the Judges what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, just one clarification. Those people who left, I thought I understood they included civilians, women and children. Among those who left, were there any armed men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that because I didn't go with them, and I don't know what any of them carried.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your village, did the Territorial Defence of the BH have a presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in your village there were only civilians, women, men, children, elderly men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So going back, then, Witness CA, to the morning of the 17th of April, can you just tell the Judges for a few moments in your own words what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first the shelling began. Shelling began of the upper part, Sovici, and then it continued on Doljani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of the morning the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the shelling continue approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 2.00, 2.30, maybe 3.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to tell - this is an area that you are very familiar with in terms of your having lived there - will you able to tell from where the shells, approximately, I'm not talking about specific, but approximately from where the shells were coming?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Risovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any villagers or any persons who were still in the village or remained in the village at that time, was anyone injured or wounded as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we could go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness CA, how far is Risovac from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 4 kilometres. Maybe a little less, maybe a little more. I never measured, but it's certainly about 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. And before the 17th of April, before 8.30 on the 17th of April, which means on the 15th and the 16th, did you know that there were units in Risovac that could fire at your village, or was it a complete surprise to you on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've just felt it on the 17th in the morning. We never knew anything before. Nobody had said anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I thought you wanted to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't think it will be necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not necessary. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, here's the evidence and I'll let the Chamber give me whatever guidance it cares to. The witness testified that there was one villager in Doljani who was wounded as a result of the shelling. Now, I'm not sure it's terribly important to know the name of this individual, but if the Chamber feels that it does, then I would go into private session and get the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness CA, the President asked you questions about whether there was an ABiH force defending the village on the 17th of April, 1993, or present in the village. Can you tell the Judges, was there any, as far as you know from what you could see or hear, was there any resistance put up by the members of the village of Doljani to the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it correct, Witness CA, that when the shelling started, approximately when the shelling started, on the morning the 17th, you remained in your house and your husband and one of your sons went to the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, why did you stay at home while your family went into the woods? Why didn't you go along with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I just stayed at home because I wasn't even afraid. I didn't know what was going on. I just stayed at home, as usual, thinking I'm going to make lunch. I wasn't afraid for myself; I was only afraid for them. I thought they should be away from home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to try to keep this to a minimum, but I think, for safety's sake, we should go back into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have got five minutes left before the break, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness CA, again, without mentioning any particular names or details, you've said already that your husband and one of your sons went into the woods around the time that the shelling started; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, without mentioning a name - I don't think for these purposes it's necessary; others can inquire if they believe that it is - was there a third man who accompanied your husband and son into the woods at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was another neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these three men, then, were any of these men carrying a weapon or firearm when they went into the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that the shelling continued until approximately 3.00 that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And around 3.00 that day, do you recall anything else happening in terms of seeing any other movement of vehicles or anything else happening that you could see from your home in Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the vehicles coming, and in them HVO uniforms. They carried weapons. And they started calling out through a loud-hailer to the population that anybody with weapons should come out; otherwise, they would shoot at civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that afternoon, did you ever see a tank in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see it, and how was it moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Going towards Sovici but going down from Risovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "going down," it was going down the hill from Risovac in the direction of Sovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we might break there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we do that, there's a question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a point of clarification. On the basis of the information we have received, we know that in the former Yugoslavia, the men were sometimes members of the Territorial Defence, and we know that at a point in time, on the Croatian side, as indeed on the Muslim side during the conflict, men from the ages of 16 to 60 were encouraged, if not obliged, to join the armed forces. Now, my question is as follows: Can you confirm that on the 17th of April, 1993, no men from your village were carrying arms, that nobody was part of the civilian defence or the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot confirm that because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, in your village, did you see neighbours going around, circulating, or locals from the village, carrying weapons in their hands? Hunting rifles, perhaps, Kalashnikovs, machine-guns, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't see any of that. When they entered -- now, I don't know when they took to the woods. I just know when my husband and son left. Now, what they had with them after that, what these people had when they came in to hand them over, I don't know. Perhaps somebody did have weapons. Somebody might have had a pistol or hunting rifle. I wasn't with them to be able to know what they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is almost 10 to 4.00. We're going to have a technical break of 20 minutes, and we're going to reconvene at exactly 10 minutes past 4.00. Before the witness leaves the courtroom to have a rest, I'd like to ask the registrar to have the blinds lowered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to clarify, we are in open session; correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, so far you've told us about the shelling that took place on the 17th of April and that later that afternoon you saw vehicles, HVO vehicles, coming into the village, and you saw a tank coming down the hill from Risovac in the direction of Sovici. Taking -- going forward from that point, what happened later that afternoon in terms of what you could observe from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon, when I saw that, I saw someone come down from Sovici, and the men gathered and took them to the Sovici school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you same the men gathered, and perhaps one thing I didn't mention and I'll be corrected if I'm wrong on this, did you say before the break that, when the HVO vehicles came into the village they were using megaphones to call out, essentially for people to come out from wherever they were and essentially surrender, give themselves up, or there would be firing on the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They called over the megaphone telling the men to surrender or they'll -- they would fire on the civilians. But they did not fire at the civilians, and the menfolk gathered together. Now, whether they would have shot, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Where did you see, then, the men who were then -- the Muslim men who were then coming out in response to this, the megaphones, where did you see them gathering and what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gathered in the centre of the village, so I was able to see them, in that village of ours. I saw four or five soldiers. I recognised two of them. I knew them, but not the third. But he was from the village, too, although I didn't know him. He was from Sovici, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, madam. You've just said that you saw four or five soldiers and that you recognised two of them. Without giving us their names, did you know their names actually, the two soldiers you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, this was probably largely addressed by a question put by the president, but just -- just so the record is clear, when you said a few moments ago that when you looked out into the centre of the village where these things were happening, you said there were four or five soldiers. Now, I'm not asking you again to give the names, which we've already dealt with in private session, but when you say there were four or five soldiers, just so it's clear, four or five soldiers of which military force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that there was anybody else but the HVO. As far as I was concerned, it was all the same, what I saw on their sleeves, the insignia there. I don't know of any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, around this time, madam, when you saw these -- the men then coming out and then coming to this central part of the village, and again without naming any names or giving any particulars at this moment, did you see your husband and son coming out as part of the men who were coming out of the woods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Not my sons and my husband. Just one son, not sons. Just one son was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I think if there was any confusion about that, I think you've clarified it. Could you see from where you were -- approximately, what was the distance from your location and where you saw the men being gathered around these HVO -- this HVO vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not 10 metres away from my house. Five metres, 10. I didn't measure it, but thereabouts. It's almost one house next to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see the types of weapons of any of the men who were coming forward, going back to what we began to touch on a few minutes ago, did you see that any of the men, including either your husband or son turned over or surrendered any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them surrender their weapons. How they did that, what they turned over, I saw all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see your -- well, first of all, did you see your husband turn over any weapon on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband didn't have a weapon at all, nor was he a member of any unit. He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask for a redaction on that point? It might be specific enough to the weapon that it might tend to identify the particular son, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you see to that, please. That means we'll have a 30-minute break during our next break. It will take us longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I regret that, Your Honour, but I didn't expect that it might come out in that particular way, but if it was my fault, then, I apologise for that. Let's go into private session, then, if we can possibly avoid the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after this time, after the weapons were turned over, among the group of men, were your -- did you see your husband and son being taken away from this area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did any of the HVO soldiers that were there, did any of them say anything to you about what was happening or would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. I just asked him what you're going to do. They said, well, if they don't come back tonight, they'll come back tomorrow. That's what the neighbour said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'm going back to what you said a moment ago, because it was the first time that I heard you say it, and as far as us Judges are concerned, it might be important. You said that the hunting rifle was returned because he had a permit. Does that mean that the hunters from your village who had a hunting rifle were obliged to have a permit to be able to carry the weapon, to have a licence for it? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My answer is no, but they took them away and nobody asked to see the permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to know is this: In your village, if a hunter -- if a man went hunting, if he was a hunter, did he have to have a permit to carry or to possess a hunting weapon, a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's what I wanted explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, just going back to -- in order to go forward again, you said that what you were told then by this HVO soldier is that they said, "Well, if they don't come back tonight, they'll come back --" in the transcript it says, "too many"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say if they didn't come back tonight you were told they would come back tomorrow, the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. And I held him to his word, but unfortunately, he only returned after 11 and a half months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we go on to the 18th, before we leave the topic of the men that were being gathered in the centre of the village, approximately, how many men did you see being gathered up in this way? Again, your best approximation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in my village?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. What you could see out in front of you, as you said, from where you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, between 15 and 20. That's how many men there were at that spot as far as I was able to see. 15 to 20 roughly, but as I say, I can't be specific, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell the Judges, please, did -- among the people that were gathered there, did you see any Muslim young men who were younger than the age of 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, three of them. Right from my village who were taken off. And there were others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how old were the three that were under the age of 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten to 15 years old, not more. Roughly 15. I don't think any of them were 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, you've already indicated that your husband in fact did not return the next day. When he did not, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to look for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the school at Sovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how far was that from your -- where you lived? Again, approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, four or five kilometres away. I don't know. I didn't measure the distance, but it's certainly that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the Sovici school, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a lot of men incarcerated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can you give us some estimate of the number of men you saw there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about a hundred if not more. Certainly a hundred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from what you could see, could you tell the Judges of what ethnic group these men, these approximately 100 or more men were, what the ethnic group of these men was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims. They didn't lock up Croats. It was the Muslims they held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see your husband at that time on this first visit to the Sovici school on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, both my husband and my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to the Sovici school later that day, and if you were with anyone else, I'm going to ask you for now not to mention any names, but my first question to you is: Did you leave the school and go back to the Sovici school later on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I returned to take them some food and clothing. However, when I returned, the situation had changed. I couldn't see them because the soldier wouldn't even let me enter the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without mentioning the person's name, when you went back to the Sovici school the second time, were you accompanied by another Muslim woman from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you travelled between Doljani and the Sovici school on the 18th of April, can you tell us what you could see in terms of the damage or the condition of the houses in Sovici and to the extent that it also included passing through Doljani? What was the condition of the houses that you could see on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all intact, in proper order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time after the 18th of April where your house and other Muslim houses in the vicinity were searched by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, quite simply they'd come to your house and force you to open the door to them so that they could search the house and do what they wanted. What they were looking for, I don't know. They didn't find anything. Now, what they were looking for, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges approximately how many times was your house - excuse me - searched in the four or five days after the attack on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten times. Not once, 10 times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Muslim men that had been held in the Sovici school that you described a few moments ago, do you know approximately when these Muslim men were taken from the Sovici school to another location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that. On the third day they took them off to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you say the third day, are you including -- say, if you include the 17th, are you saying on approximately the 19th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know at the time or did you learn later where the Muslim men that were in the Sovici school as of that time, where they were taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learnt that later when I went to look for them on the third day. Then a woman told me that they were dragged off during the night, but they didn't know where. We didn't know where either straight away. Two days later, somebody came and told us that they were at Ljubuski, Ljubusko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, continuing on about the 19th or 20th of April, did anything happen to the Muslim houses in Sovici and Doljani around that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as they took them away, they set fire to all the houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "all the houses," which houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness CA, do you know if there were any Croat houses that were set on fire during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The houses that were set on fire, do you know what happened to the occupants of those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took them to the school at Sovici. They took the men to Ljubuski, and the civilians and elderly, women, and children, they were put in the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other group of houses in the area of Sovici and Doljani that remained undamaged that were then -- excuse me, that were then used for the purposes of holding Muslim civilians in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In two places. Seven houses in one place and in another place four houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The seven houses, that was a location or a gathering of houses that is sometimes referred to as the Junuzovici houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the name or reference for the other location, for the four houses, for the grouping of four houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called Krkaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, during this time period when some of the Muslim people had been taken to the Sovici school, to your knowledge, were any Muslims held for a time in the Doljani mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They held them in the mosque during the time they were setting fire to their houses, and then they took them off to that village Krkaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything to your knowledge happen to the mosque once the Muslims that had been held there were taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was blown up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard the detonation, the explosion, but I didn't know what was going on. And later on I heard that it had been mined, that it was blown up. But the explosion was so strong that you could hear if far and wide.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some point learn from your neighbours or friends that -- that in fact the explosion that you heard at that time had been the Doljani mosque being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there also a mosque in Sovici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you travelled between your house and the Sovici school on the 18th of April, did you pass by the mosque in Sovici or did you travel in such a way that you could see the mosque in Sovici at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't pass by the mosque when I went to visit my husband and son at the school building. Well, then I saw that it was still standing, but later on it had been blown up. It didn't exist any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- and I was taking it step-by-step. That's why I asked you on the 18th of April when you went -- when you travelled to visit your husband at the Sovici school, I take it from your answer just now, that you saw the mosque on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you've indicated it, again, if we just make clear for the record, what was the condition of the Sovici mosque when you saw it on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was all right on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've already indicated that your house was searched a number of times. Did there come a time in the four, five, or six days after the 17th that you were told to leave your house, that you would have -- that you would have to go to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell the Judges about that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My neighbours came and they said, "You have to go to the school. We've received orders to take you all to the school," and that's what we did. We had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened once you got to the Sovici school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was horrible. Crammed in two rooms there were so many women, men, elderly men, children. It was pure horror.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to those of you who were coming to the Sovici school on that day, including yourself? What -- what, if anything, did you have to do or was done when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. They just called us out, asked where we'd come from, and we signed something. I wasn't there more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you say they asked you where you came from and you signed something, is it correct, Witness CA, that they were listing you or registering you, if you will, and the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall the name of any particular HVO soldier who was involved in making this list or taking this registration?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, we can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
