utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I believe we can take that without implicating the confidentiality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of that HVO soldier, if you knew, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Blaz Azinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you travelled around the Doljani-Sovici area at that time, at approximately how many days after the 17th was it? Again, as best as you can, please. How many days after the 17th, when you went to the Sovici -- when you were told to go to the Sovici school for the purpose of being registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe four days, not more. Four or five days, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can we understand that it was approximately around the 21st or 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you travelled between your home and the Sovici school on the 21st or 22nd of April, did you see anything different about the Muslim houses in that area, different than what you had seen on the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the registration at the Sovici school, were a number of the Muslim women and children kept at the Junuzovici houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, how many would you say were altogether held in the seven houses there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there were about 400.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us about just the situation as to those houses. What was -- were you free to move about? What were the conditions? What happened when you were being held in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was horrible. We didn't dare move. Nobody dared to move from one house to another. And how can one feel in that situation? So little room for so many people. We had no proper living conditions. There was no electricity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HVO soldiers ever fire their weapons at the house, at the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially at night after having a few drinks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what. They would shoot, knock at doors, ask for girls, all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "ask for girls," can you tell the Judges more about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. They wanted the girls to come out. Nobody was taken away from my house. I hid my girls day and night. They didn't go out at all. But they took girls away from other houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know, Witness, you don't want to say too much about this and I'm not going to ask you in any great detail, but do you know if any of the girls came back to the houses --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, we're now back in open session. You started to give an answer. You said, "While we were in our houses, no. After we left, I don't know what they did." At any time did you lose any -- during this time period, did you lose any of the vehicles or livestock that you and your family owned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. All the livestock and all the cars were taken away, but nothing was taken away outside the houses when we were there. Everybody's cars were driven away, and livestock as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to confront one of the HVO soldiers about this happening and why this was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would only tell us they had orders. From whom, I don't know. Whatever you asked them, they would say, "We have orders."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they give you any indication in terms of these orders what was supposed to be done with this property, the vehicles and livestock that were seized?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you personally, did you lose any livestock and one car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did HVO soldiers give you some sort of document like a receipt confirming the requisition of that livestock and the vehicle, or did they give you nothing whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you say that when you asked an HVO soldier -- soldier or soldiers, they replied they had orders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your village, did you have the impression that this HVO soldier -- that these soldiers were under some sort of command? Was there anybody who looked like he was in control of the soldiers, that he was their commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, because under whose orders would they be acting then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you think, but you have nothing to confirm that there was a commander on the spot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I cannot do. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that regard, Witness CA, and I was about to ask you, during this time you were being held in the houses when you saw these things happening, when the property was being taken, did you hear the name Tuta, or did you hear that people called Tuta's men were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you hear that, and what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, an occasional soldier would come and say that he was a Tuta's soldier. Some others wouldn't say that. His name was mentioned, and some even had his photograph on their windscreen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving forward, then. Around the 5th of May, 1993, what happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They drove us out of our houses, made us get into vehicles, and took us to Risovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you give us a bit more detail, please, on how that happened? Were you loaded on vehicles? Were you made to walk? How did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They drove us by freight vehicles. Up there buses were waiting. And then they loaded us onto buses and hauled us across Mount Vran up to a petrol station where they unloaded us. The name of that petrol station was Sicaja. That remained etched in my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This petrol station, approximately where was it located with reference to the two towns of Prozor on the one hand and Gornji Vakuf on the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's somewhere in between, on top of a hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we come back to that, you said a moment ago that, "They drove us by freight vehicles."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that another description for trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many trucks were involved in moving these approximately 400 Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trips did it take for these trucks to get all of you to the top of Risovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the top of Risovac you were then transferred onto buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how many buses were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Seven -- some people said seven, others said six, but there couldn't have been less because we were so many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, the drivers of those buses, were they Muslims or Croats, soldiers? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldiers. They were all dressed as soldiers. In every bus there were three or four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the driver was also dressed as a soldier in a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Each of them had a weapon close by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And from what you know, where did those buses come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where they came from to Risovac. I only know they were waiting for us there. They could have come from Duvno, Mostar. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A transfer of that amount of the population, because there were apparently 400 people, can you think of any reason why, since you were moving from point A to point B, they would make you move? Was it for your own safety? Was it for some health or sanitary reason? Did they give you any reason, or did they say nothing at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't say anything. Only that they had orders to make us leave. They told us to take things that we need from our houses and, "You will never come back." That's what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can imagine that on the buses -- you said on the buses there were drivers in uniform who had a weapon handy, and there were another three or four soldiers on every bus, so I suppose the villagers spoke to the soldiers, asked them questions like, "What's going on? Where are we going?" Were there any such conversations between the soldiers and the villagers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my bus, the one I was on, nobody asked anything, nor did they dare ask. If the soldier was a bit drunk, he would immediately turn on you and point his gun. Some even got angry because children were crying. I don't know about the other buses. In mine, nobody asked a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody asked anything, but you suppose that if a soldier was drunk -- what made you think they were drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Well, I saw it. I was there. Because a sober man would not be acting like that. He would not have the same expression on his face. After all, there were women and children on the buses. You could see. It was obvious he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was one who was drunk or they were all drunk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one who was cursing and swearing was certainly drunk. Those who kept silent, I don't know. They didn't utter a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those HVO soldiers, were they from the same locality or were they from further away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know a single one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But from their accent, from their conduct, their intonation, their voices, would you place them in your region or some other area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not from our area. They had a lilt in their speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what made you think they were not from your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know the dialect of my own neighbours, and I know the difference between that particular speech and speech of people outside. They had a different accent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say it's the level of accent, and you noticed certain differences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us an example, maybe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. Some would say "reka" instead of "reko" for the word "said," and some of our neighbours placed them in an area called Zagorje. Anyway, they were not from our region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on that, you said just now, ma'am, that some of the neighbours placed, at least the linguistic distinctions, placed them in an area called Zagorje. Can you tell the Judges, if you know, where that location was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, because I never went that way, but I heard other people say, "He's speaking like a Zagorac, meaning a region called "Croatian Zagorje." Where exactly it is, I don't know. I've often heard tale of this Croatian Zagorje, but I don't know exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've said that you were driven in these buses over mountain Vran, if I've heard correctly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact -- the group of you, did you spend the night on Mount Vran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two buses broke down and we couldn't go on, and the people from those two buses could not be crammed into the other buses because all of them were full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what time the next day did you arrive at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. They just unloaded us, and they said, "You have your Alija. He'll take care of you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went back, and we were left to our own devices. Some people went on on foot. We didn't really know where to go and what to do, but somehow we reached Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the whole group of you walk as far as Gornji Vakuf, or did at some point you receive some assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They got assistance. Somebody sent a message up there and people came down to fetch them with cars. Some went on on foot and others were taken in vehicles, so all of us made it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately how long did you and, to the extent you know, the other Muslims that were taken to Gornji Vakuf that day or toward Gornji Vakuf, how long did you stay in Gornji Vakuf at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I returned on the 6th of June, and the others stayed on for a couple of more days. I returned to Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you return -- or excuse me. Did you live, then, in Jablanica during the remainder of the war, at least through 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Jablanica for 11 and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your husband and son, again, without going into any more details, can you tell the Judges approximately when they were released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were released on the 1st of March, after 11 and a half months. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. In the transcript, there was a mistake when the witness said that I lived in Jablanica for 11 and a half years. Most probably it was one and a half years, I believe. May we clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think from talking to the witness, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you heard the Judge's question, Witness CA. Can you tell the Judges whether it was in fact correct that you did remain in Jablanica for the next 11 and a half years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us -- you said your husband and son were released on the 1st of March. Just so the record is clear, when you say the 1st of March, was that 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for one moment, Your Honour. Just -- partly to assist Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a few moments we are going to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, I'd like to finish your testimony by looking at four documents which I can see there's a bundle of material sitting on the witness stand there next to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Usher, would you please help the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I please ask the witness to first look at Exhibit 2009. When you have that, Witness, can you please look at the paragraph -- if you can find the paragraph that starts with "Almost all the Muslim houses are set on fire in Sovici." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Continue down the page, please, until you get to that paragraph after a reference to Ostrozac. Exhibit 2009. If you go down the left side of the page, Witness, until you find the words "Almost all the Muslim houses are set on fire." And I realise in the translation the word order may be different than --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And looking to that entire paragraph which then continues on and that paragraph ends with the words "The direction of Posusje and Tomislavgrad." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is what is stated in that paragraph, Witness, is that consistent with what you saw and experienced in the second half of April, 1993, in Sovici-Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph goes on to talk about European Community observers. Do you recall at any time where members -- excuse me, representatives of the international community attempted to enter or did enter the area of Sovici-Doljani in the second half of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They entered and reach the Sovici school, but where the civilians were, they didn't allow them to get to there and to tour that area where we were. Just the old men who were in the school. They made a list of them, but nobody came to see us civilians, where we were, where the women and children were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- you said just now, you said "where the civilians were, they didn't allow them to go." Who didn't allow them to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who didn't allow them to go? I don't know. The people standing guard over us hoped they would come, but who didn't allow them to come I don't know. They made us all go outside and lined us up and said, "Be careful what you say, because they're going to leave but you're going to stay." That's what they told us. Now, why they didn't arrive and why somebody didn't let them come, I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see UNPROFOR vehicles in the area around this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you said a moment ago that they told you to -- said, "Be careful what you say," who said that? I don't necessarily mean the individuals, but were these the HVO guards around the houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO guards, but I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look next at Exhibit 2063 in the same bundle you have there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, madam. You said a moment ago that the HVO guards hoped that the internationals would come to see you and that's why they lined you up, and it turned out they didn't come. Now, can you confirm that the HVO guards, at first, wanted you to meet these foreigners who were coming to see what was going on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they hoped they'd come. I think they thought they would come. Now, who prevented them from coming I don't know, because if they hadn't hoped they would come they wouldn't have taken us out and lined us up. And they said to us, "Careful what you say" because they're going to leave, but you're going to stay. That's what we were told. Now, why they didn't come and who didn't let them come, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be -- there might be a translation error in your language, because they said that they were expecting them to come or they were hoping. Expecting and hoping isn't the same thing. When one says one hopes then one would like something to happen, but when one expects them to come, one might expect people to come whom you don't want to see. So could you tell me what the HVO soldiers actually said with respect to the arrival of the internationals? Was it hoped or was it that they were expecting a visit from the internationals, not necessarily liking it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't explain that because we didn't know anything until they took us outside, and then I saw that they went to Sovici. I could see that part of the road. They said, "They'll come here. Be careful of what you say." Now, whether they thought they would be coming or didn't think they would be coming, nobody explained that. But they thought they would come, because they wouldn't then line us up outside and say what they said to us. Now, why they didn't turn up, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are the Judges then to understand that you were placed on the ready and that you were told what you were allowed to say to those internationals and what not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that's it. That would be it. Because they said, "Be careful what you say." So I suppose they were expecting them to ask us something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, if we then could go to the next exhibit, Exhibit 2063. In that document, Witness, there's the statement, "We have a total of 422 women and children and 25 conscripts." Is the description and the number of 422 women and children, is that basically consistent with the information that you had at the time or what you actually saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next -- very next sentence says, "Also 94 conscripts were transported to Ljubuski." Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not all of them were conscripts. There were some older people there too. There were even some people who were born in 1936, 1938, 1940, and older. So they weren't conscripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your husband was among this group, you've told us. Did you consider him to be a conscript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further down it makes the statement that, "The Muslim houses were burnt -- were burnt down and two mosques were demolished." Is that statement consistent with what you saw and heard in Sovici-Doljani in mid-April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- this document is signed or at least over the name, has been prepared above the name of Marko Rozic. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without saying anything that might tend to identify yourself, Witness, do you know anything about Mr. Rozic and his involvement in these matters at that time, that is, in the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know nothing of his involvement or any of the positions he occupied or didn't occupy. I just know him personally. And I assume he was in some position where people asked him about things, if these documents were in his possession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know -- did you have any basis to know what Mr. Rozic's views were of the relationships between the Muslims and the Croats at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you next, please, to look at Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, madam. The Prosecutor has just asked you a question, but it requires some more specific information. You said that you knew this man, Mr. Marko Rozic. Now, the Judges would like to know whether this was a Croat or a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So you said you knew him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he one of the inhabitants of your village or what? How did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He lived in Sovici. He was an inhabitant of Sovici, and my sons used to see him a lot and socialise. They would go to see him. He would come to see them. So I know him, and I know the whole family, his whole family. I was born in Sovici, too, myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There we have it. Thank you for giving us that additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could then go to Exhibit 2200. It's a very short document, madam, and if you could just look at that. It's really only one sentence -- well, two. Were you, in fact, among those who were transported on buses from the area of Sovici-Doljani on approximately the 5th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was transported with those buses, yes. It wasn't Doljani-Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I'm going to ask you to read the paragraph out, because in the English translation, there's a word that I am querying. So I'd like you to read the paragraph out in your own language and the interpreters are going to interpret it. And it begins with the word "Da."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure I can see this properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Are there literally five buses in Sovici or Doljani? The population taken towards Jablanica. If that's not correct. If there are, then that's not correct." No. It says, "If they were, where did they come from?" I don't know whether they were from Duvno, Mostar, Posusje. I don't know. There are roads all over the place. But they didn't come from Jablanica, I know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, there's a word in brackets, "zelene." What does that word mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea what that means there. "Taken away" perhaps, "odevzeni." With a letter missing. And then it turned out to be "zelene." "Odevzeni" and then it turned out as "zelene." "Zelene towards Jablanica." I think it means "odevzeni" or "driven towards," "transported towards Jablanica," but that's just not correct. I don't know who signed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in English it says "green." The word is translated as "green." Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does it say here, "Petkovic," "Petrovic"? I can't make it out. I really can't make head or tail of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before moving to the final document, can I just ask you, apart from the fact that you indicated that you did not in fact, on this occasion, go toward Jablanica, but instead toward Gornji Vakuf, is the rest of what's said there essentially descriptive of what happened to you and the others on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 2191. The last document in the bundle, I hope. Very briefly, I think. Looking at the first paragraph of that document which starts "Today at around 9.00, approximately 300 persons," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see it very well. I'm afraid these glasses aren't much use. I can see far away but not close to. I can't make out the letters really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do the best you can, please. Can you see the reference, for example, to the Sicaj petrol station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hope I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the first paragraph, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sicaja, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that consistent with the name of the petrol station that you gave to the Judges a few minutes ago as to where you were taken then put off the buses at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on that document, Witness CA, down to the left of the signature part or the name, at least, you have Uskoplje 551993. The Judges have probably heard this already, but just to be clear, was Uskoplje the Croat name given to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness CA, I want to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for assisting us this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could you do the calculations. How much time have the Prosecution taken? Unfortunately, we're going to have to have a 30-minute break for the redaction to be made possible, and we'll reconvene at five to 6.00. I'd like to state that the Prosecutor took up 71 minutes. So I hope the Defence will be able to get through their cross-examination and not have the witness return tomorrow for just a few minutes. We'll reconvene at five to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to start off the cross-examination. Madam, if you have any difficulties or aren't feeling well, don't hesitate to let us know. If you don't feel able to continue, tell me straight away and we'll take the necessary steps. Who is going to start off on the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we have no questions for the witness. We'd like to thank the witness for coming to give her evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not have any questions for this witness either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Praljak Defence have no questions for this witness, but Mr. Praljak would like to ask only one question about the language since the Prosecutor was mentioning something about one dialect of the Croatian languages. Just to enlighten everybody. But it would be on the end or he can do it now. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor mentioned that one of the men who escorted the buses, according to what the witness told us, spoke -- or, rather, they referred to him as Zagorac and that he spoke the kind of language that would mean that he was from an area called Hrvatsko/Croatian Zagorje. Now, in the Croatian Zagorje, the language spoken there is a language which is called Kirkovski. It isn't a dialect of the Croatian language, it is a separate language which is completely incomprehensible to a large number of Croats not living in the area. That's one point. And I'm going to ask a question. But when we consider the notion of Zagorac, which includes the word "gora," and "gora" means a "hill" in Croatian and everything across a hill, over the hill, people say are Zagorje, over the hill. So Dalmatian Zagorje is behind Mount Velebit, Bjelusine and so on. So we have a lot of these Zagorjes; 20 or 30. Each place has its own Zagorje or area behind the hill and beyond the hill. And I'm sure the interpreters won't be able to translate what I'm saying now. In the Croatian Zagorje, and I'm going to quote a writer, he says as follows, it is from a poem: [No interpretation] Cross-examination by the Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, did you understand any of what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or another piece of poetry. Let me just remember how it goes. It never was that -- it wasn't somehow, so in the future it will be somehow, one way or another, because that's how things always were. Things were always somehow established. Did the man speak that kind of language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him speak in the Zagorje language. He didn't speak to me. I saw him speak to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it is very difficult for anybody to understand that language, and I don't think the interpreters could have understood it either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, the last poem that you recited seemed to be quite a witty one. One day you might do us the pleasure and give us the translation. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] It's very simple, Your Honour. It says things always happen in one way or another. They always happen. Because things happened in the past and things were settled in the past, they -- and in the future, things will somehow work out too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's a quotation from probably the most valuable Croatian literary work or author. His name was Miroslav Krleza, and I think his works have been translated into many different languages. But the fact is that this is a dialect and it's difficult to translate a dialect, of course. It is a dialect of the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you to you too. And I'm interested in more, but I think it would be abusing the Chamber's time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have a few questions for the witness. I'd like to emphasise, so that there's no misunderstanding, that I did hand in two documents to the Trial Chamber which I might refer to but later on when I come to challenge the authenticity of one document shown by the Prosecutor. I'm just going to ask the witness a few questions. But as I am going to mention names, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, good afternoon. I'm going to ask you something very briefly on behalf of General Petkovic, who is my client in this trial.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I took care to be in private session on these questions, Your Honour. I think we should again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I thought that the question was general enough for us not to be able to identify the witness, but I have nothing against moving into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move back into private session. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it have its -- its unit in the village of Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the neighbouring village of Sovici, was there a BH army unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that either. I never asked anybody, nor did anybody talk to me about that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO as you put it here, did the HVO exist in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know about them until the day the attack was launched. Whether it existed or not, I really don't know. But when the village was attacked, then I knew that the HVO existed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the soldiers came and introduced themselves, and everybody had those patches on their uniforms. They had weapons as well. That's how I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, we need to be in private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please do the necessary to redact the question referring to the son and we're going to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't want to interrupt but, because we have a short pause, can I also ask for a redaction please on page 86, lines 9 to 13. It was right before we went into private session previously when a couple of things were said. It shouldn't cause a delay because this should be our last session of the day, but I would ask for that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please check, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you two women alone walked on that day four or five kilometres one way and the same distance back. And I believe for everybody in this courtroom, including the Trial Chamber, it is important to find out what happened on that road. Did you see any military units stationary or movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw their vehicles moving. Around the schoolhouse there was a lot of troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please describe the road to Sovici? And when we get to Sovici, we'll deal with that description. For the moment, you are walking from Doljani to Sovici. Did you see movements of any armed units? Did you see any tanks, cannons? What did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You couldn't see that when you walked, but I saw that on the day of the attack, a tank coming down from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But what did you see on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not much, just their vehicles and troops on vehicles. They did not intercept us. They did not provoke us in any way. They just let us walk in peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the number of the vehicles or troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not looking for an exact number. Was there a convoy, 50?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that there were 10 or 15 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around that number.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jeeps, for the most part, or military vans.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, maybe, how many people there were in each of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How large were those vehicles? What was their holding capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I know nothing about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear shelling of another area? Did you hear any noise that would indicate that there was fighting in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I even saw shells falling, although, until that day, I didn't see what a -- I didn't know what a shell was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where did you see shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, they fell on Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, no. Leave alone the 18th -- the 17th. We're talking about the 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would there be fighting on the 18th? They wouldn't be fighting each other, would they?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So on that day there was no fighting that you noticed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like now to discuss with you this evacuation of the residents of Doljani. Tell me, please, did there come a time when you were visited by any kind of delegation, military or civilian, on behalf of the Croatian army, the HVO, or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina to ask you about your health and if you need anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you hear that, in the beginning of May, the main man of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina came to that area, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, and the commander of HVO, my client, Mr. Petkovic, accompanied by foreign observers, did you hear of their presence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but only on the bus in Vran. Those people, our escorts, were talking and saying that Sefer Halilovic and this defendant of yours --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, Witness, did you hear what they were talking about there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear maybe what kind of agreement was reached between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Why would anybody tell me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, the person who told you about their visit to Sovici could have told you that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a Croatian soldier on the bus in Vran.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did that Croatian soldier tell you on the bus at that moment because that was agreed between Halilovic and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he wasn't talking to me at all in the first place. The soldiers were talking amongst themselves. I was just sitting nearby and overheard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you conclude from their conversation that all of that was organised because that was agreed between Halilovic and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They didn't say anything about that. They only said that these men had come to the schoolhouse. Nobody mentioned any agreement. One of the men interrupted the other and said, "I know," and there was no more talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to remind you of a document that you have seen recently. It is signed by my client, Milivoj Petkovic. It concerns that group of five buses, if you remember it. If you don't remember it, we can look at the document again. It's P 02200. According to that document, the question is asked concerning those buses that were to drive the residents of Sovici and Doljani towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Although I understand from your answers that you couldn't be aware of the agreements, is it logical that this question about buses to Jablanica was asked because there was an agreement to organise those buses to Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no clue. If there was an agreement, then why did they drag us back?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I think this has gone on long enough. The witness has repeatedly said she doesn't know. And the same question has been put over and over again, I think, and especially in the interest of time, I think that we should move on to something more significant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, if you are producing this document, is it that you want to send a message to the Trial Chamber that there was an agreement between Petkovic and Halilovic whereby your client envisaged a transport for these persons? Is that the point?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the course of questioning Mr. Idrizovic, we produced a document from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina reflecting meetings and the visit to Sovici on the 4th of May, 1993, and from that document, it clearly follows that there was an agreement between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic, that those residents of Doljani and Sovici would be evacuated to Jablanica. From other documents and some pending documents that will later be introduced through witnesses from this locality, it will be clear that people in Doljani and Sovici were asked where they wanted to go, whether some of them wanted to go home, perhaps, and they said they wanted to go to Jablanica, and that's why the buses were placed at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered reluctantly, and let me put it once again. On the 4th of May, Generals Halilovic and Petkovic met and reached an agreement. According to that agreement, the residents of Doljani and Sovici were to be transported to Jablanica. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, why didn't they comply with that agreement? If I may ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We'll try to establish that later. That's why I started with this document to see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the Prosecutor is right. We're absolutely getting nowhere, and I must tell you that I can also not see at all, not from far away, how the document 2200 proves any agreement. It is a question. Your client does not know where buses come from. That's what it says, and it's -- it's really rather difficult to understand, frankly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I just said is not proven by this document. I referenced another document of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is in fact a report on what happened on the 4th of May, 1993. This document is not here now, but it states clearly that there was an agreement. It's a document we used with witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could we agree that we stick to the documents that we have, because it's complicated enough as it is, and to refer to documents that we do not have, is not conducive to the establishment of the truth, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that this document has not been prepared for this witness, because I did not originally intend to ask this question of her in this way, but at this moment, my intention is to establish why those people were not taken to Jablanica directly and why they instead went to Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that something you're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No. I'll try to proceed slowly and maybe we'll come to an answer. Tell me, during your trip, did you go by the road from Doljani to Jablanica at least part of the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which road did the buses take immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses were at Risovac, and we were brought to them by trucks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when did the buses set off from Risovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went towards Duvno. I don't know. It was night-time. We were going generally towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did anybody stop you on the road? Were there any check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How would I know?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why would they stop us? There were no check-point of ours. There were only Croats there. Who would stop their buses? They knew perfectly well what was going on, where we were going, where we were being driven. If they didn't know, why would they have left us at Sicaja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Following up on the question asked by Ms. Alaburic, she intended to prove through documents that you were to go to Jablanica. Tell us, that road that you took, then, was it the direct, shortest way to Jablanica or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say no. Why wasn't it the shortest, direct way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The shortest way is steep uphill, and we didn't take that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't take that road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Never mind, Witness. We'll try to establish what exactly happened through other witnesses. Now, I would like to clarify some details concerning your house in Doljani. Tell me, your house in Doljani was not damaged on the day of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your house was not even damaged at the moment when you were leaving Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After leaving Doljani, you first saw your house again three years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And only then did you see that it was damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened around Doljani in the meantime? For instance, are you aware that in July, 1993, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina captured Doljani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that, is it fair to conclude that your house was neither damaged nor destroyed in that April or May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I would like us to look at another document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor earlier today. It's 2063.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 2063. I just don't understand why I have to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No, you don't have to read it. I will do that. I will read the part that is relevant to my question. One passage that the Prosecutor didn't show you, which is the last one in this first paragraph. It says: "After the cessation of hostilities in this area, all Muslim houses were set on fire and two mosques were destroyed under orders of superior commanders." What I'm interested in are the words "under orders of superior commanders." But before I ask my question, please bear with me while I give you a brief introduction, which will also contain some information relevant for the record. In the closing arguments in the trial against Tuta Naletilic on the 28th of October, 2002, in the transcript, page 1660 and the next page, 1661, the Prosecutor said the following verbatim: "Precisely with reference to this document and retelling its contents," and that document in that trial was Exhibit P333, he said, "The highest commander in that operation was Tuta Naletilic." You, madam, also mentioned the name of Tuta today apart from the things you've already told us. From what you know, was Tuta some sort of commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You cannot tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Some soldiers did come and said they were Tuta's soldiers. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any difference between your local people from the HVO and the men who introduced themselves as belonging to Tuta's units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were extremely strict and harsh with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who said they were Tuta's soldiers. There was a big difference between the neighbours who stood guard over us and the time when they were replaced by Tuta's soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did they come on the 21st of April, like four or five days after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Tuta's deputy got killed and that's why Tuta's men were very nervous, and they wanted to go into action? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him, "Why is this going on? Why are you setting the village on fire?" And he said, "Tuta's soldier got killed."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did they mention his name? Was it maybe Cikota?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that the man who got killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just remember that the name was mentioned. Whether it was his or somebody else who got killed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions, unless my client has something to add. No. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to clarify one point, Witness. You said that, at the outset, you could confirm that your house was not damaged or destroyed in April or May because the ABiH took over in -- July, and you said your house could not have been destroyed in that period. Now, speaking of Tuta's soldiers, you say on page 105, line 19, that you asked a soldier, "Why are you setting the village on fire?" And the soldier answered, "Well, because one of Tuta's men was killed." So the conclusion is that when you're asking this question it's April and the village is on fire or burnt down. So when you say that the village was burnt down, was it Doljani, your village, that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, Doljani and Sovici. I asked them why they had set fire to the villages. I meant both the villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Fine. Now, the two villages, Doljani and Sovici, were set on fire in what month according to you? When was that? What month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the conflict. As soon as they took the men to Ljubuski, they started setting fire to the village -- villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, after the conflict, what date would that be exactly? Would that be the 18th, 19th, 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the 19th, 20th, 21st, somewhere around there. I would say that it was probably the 20th. I don't remember the dates because there were a lot of awful things going on, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... take too much time, but this issue can probably be clarified as follows: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: (redacted). Isn't it right that some of the houses probably belonged to your family, relatives? They were not burnt down but there in those houses about 400 -- yes, I'm sorry. I did mention the name. But anyway, it is important, because as far as I remember, during the first hours of the questions and answers, it was mentioned that these houses were kept and about 400 people had been crammed or crowded there. So it is my question, if it was one of the reasons why your house has not been burnt, but it was in a way probably later on when it happened. So it is my question that -- that that is the issue here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's it, yes, because two months later -- two months after everything my house was set on fire. After we had left, two months later our house was burnt down and the other seven -- well, where the civilians were put up, the women, the children, two months later, the houses, our houses, were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said two months later your house was burnt down. Now, as far as the Judges are concerned, we have to establish who torched your house, the HVO or the BH army. According to you, who was it who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the BH army couldn't reach my house at all. Doljani hadn't been attacked then when they set fire to this two months later. It couldn't have been anybody else except the HVO. Now, who exactly, I can't say. I'd like to know that myself, who actually set fire to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Madam, a while ago, questioned by counsel, you have said that you left Doljani with your house intact and you never got back until three years later and, that in the meantime, the ABiH had taken Doljani. The implication of this was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The implication of this, of course, is that it is possible that your house was burned down by the ABiH. But right now, you have said that three months after you have left, your house was burned down. On what information do you base this assertion? How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that. I know who stayed on in the other villages, those belonging to Prozor. They couldn't stay there any more because they began to ask for them, and the people who would go at night across that territory, I was told by them that our houses were set fire to. So that's how I deduced that it was two months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you -- could you tell us the names of the person or persons or person who told you this, and if so, just say yes or no, because we would then go into private session to hear them. Who told you? Can you tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I suggest that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session. But, Mr. Registrar, do what is necessary to redact the houses and the names belonging to her family.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, you told us today that on that second occasion when you went to the school at Sovici, you took with you food and clothing; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were you able to leave the food and clothing you had taken over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the soldier didn't allow me to enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My second question is this: Tell me, please, when did the men from your house go to the woods? I'm not saying which men on purpose. We know who they are. Was it the day before the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. When they went -- what would they be doing in the woods before the village had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When they went to the woods, what happened to the weapons under the bed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So they took the weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They took the weapons with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that because previously you said you didn't know whether they were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took the weapons with them but they didn't shoot.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were you in the woods with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not. But they did not shoot. And this was just 15 metres away from my own house. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott, any additional questions? No? Perhaps you have some documents to tender. Can you give us the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Consistent with, I guess, the developing practice, we have prepared a sheet. I have not had a chance to distribute it yet, but I will. But the numbers are Exhibit P 02009, P 02063, P 02191, and P 02200. And perhaps with the usher's assistance I can tender this to the registry and it can be given an IC number has been the practice. Excuse me for a moment. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, give us a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be Exhibit number IC 77, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Does the Defence wish to tender any documents? No. I understand it that they do not. Fine. Now, madam, your -- yes, is there a document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no documents to be tendered, but I have an objection to one of the exhibits, but I'd like to challenge its authenticity, but my explanation would last longer than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is that? What document? No. Just a minute. The Judges are professionals and they'll be able to understand your objections in three minutes. What document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be difficult to do that in three minutes because I have to show you two exhibits in order to explain why I am objecting and it is P 02063 that I'm objecting to. It is the last exhibit that we were discussing. Can we have the document on e-court for a moment, P 02063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have it in front of us. Now, why are you challenging that?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm challenging the authenticity of the document because I consider that this document was not compiled by Marko Rozic, and I would like to indicate some of the details which are obvious, spring to view immediately. If you look at the memorandum or immediately underneath the number, the protocol number, it says "defence department," "department of defence" and you will see that it is the representative of the department of defence which assigns this and it's not the same department. That's a notorious fact. Now, in what was shown to the witness today, that portion, it was stated that all the Muslim houses were set on fire, and this witness told us today indubitably that the Junuzovici houses remained intact along with four other houses where they were put up. In order to show that it is an exhibit which was not authentic and was not signed by Mr. Rozic, I would like, if possible, is to take a look at and have placed on e-court a document that was signed by Mr. Rozic to compare the two documents and you'll be able to see that the signatures are different. It is document 3D 00563. Their Honours have the document before them, the hard copy of the document, and by comparing the two signatures, they will be able to conclude, and we can leave this Croatian document with the signature on e-court and just -- and place the second document on e-court with Marko Rozic's signature, so that we can compare the two. Furthermore, I would like to have shown another document on e-court, 3D 00562. It is a report from Mostar dated the 23rd of April, 1993, compiled at 1800 hours. And from that document, we can see that the person in question who would have been signed or, as it says in P 00263, that the document was signed by Marko Rozic, the report relates to the 23rd of April, 1993, at 12 hours -- 1200 hours. From document 3D 00562, that is to say, the report, we can see that Marko Rozic, on the 23rd of April, was held up at the check-point by the tobacco factory in Mostar. He was held there by the military police of the BH army. They asked for his credentials, wrote down his name, and detained him there for the next few hours. So that he was detained at 10.00. I'm trying to speed up, so I'm not going to read through this whole document. You have the document in front of us. He was detained at 10.30 hours. It says what procedure was applied, and Marko Rozic, therefore, on the 24th or, rather, the 23rd of April at 12.00 could not have been in Jablanica and could not have compiled the other document. I would also like to indicate that the document was the subject of discussion in the Tuta and Stela trial, and I'd like to refer to the transcript of the 14th of October, 2002, the page number is 16489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, in order to speed up, you say that the document was the subject of discussion in the previous trial. I understood it that it was admitted under P333, that that was the number it was admitted under. So what you've said is that there was already a discussion on that issue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right. Regardless of that, I know that it was adopted and admitted into evidence under the number P333. I am nonetheless highlighting these elements. It is my right to do so, and all I want to say is that the witness in the Tuta and Stela trial was shown this document and the witness said that it was not Rozic's signature and another document was shown him [as interpreted] from which they were able to see that that was an authentic signature. So I wish to challenge the authenticity of this exhibit based on the documents that were presented here today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We've understood your objection, and the Chamber will deliberate on the matter. Thank you, madam, for coming to testify here, called by the Prosecution. Thank you for testifying about the events that took place in your locality. On behalf of my colleagues, I wish you all the best in returning home to your country. Before you leave, we have to lower the blinds once again. And we adjourn for the day and start at 2.15 tomorrow with another witness. There will be three hours of examination-in-chief and three hours of cross-examination. I wish you all a very pleasant evening and would like to tell you that the Chamber has -- will have a decision on the duration of the trial which we invite you to read when you have the time to do so. Thank you. We reconvene tomorrow afternoon at 2.15.
